...New 12Z Aviation Discussion...

.KEY MESSAGES...
 
  - Unseasonably warm conditions will continue into the beginning

    to mid 100s Today and Sunday.

  - Continued increased moisture across the region will keep

.SHORT TERM...
(Today through Sunday)
Issued at 329 AM EDT Sat Sep 19 2026

High pressure wedge/ridge continue to weaken and moisture pushes 
SW down the eastern seaboard. This increased moisture combined 
with high temps in the lower to middle 90s will keep precip 
chances elevated through the weekend. A weak backdoor cold front 
along the NC/SC border will keep moving SW and push into east GA 
this afternoon. A decent amount of low to mid level moisture will 
accompany this boundary as Dewpoints expected in the 70s across 
North and Central GA Today. Combined with an axis of moderate 
instability we will see scattered to numerous showers and 
thunderstorms this afternoon and evening. Low level lapse rates 
expected to become fairly steep again this afternoon so looks like
the greatest threat from any storms that develop will be strong 
gusty winds again. We will also see frequent lightning strikes and
periods of heavy rain.

Ongoing showers over the eastern plains early this morning will
steadily dissipate as we near sunrise, while moisture will
continue feeding into the high country this morning where showers
will linger. Despite modestly cooler conditions today (highs will
remain below 80F over the plains), we'll hold onto moderately 
unstably conditions and ample moisture. The latest forecast 
soundings indicate bulk shear of 35-50 kts across the majority of 
the plains this afternoon, which would support another round of 
numerous thunderstorms, some of which will be strong to severe. 
Thus far, there isn't much indication of low stratus this morning,
so don't foresee convective temperatures not being reached. 
Instability will be exceedingly marginal though for areas roughly 
along and west of I-25, so the potential for stronger storms and 
heavier rainfall will be considerably tapered outside of our rural
plains. Hail and heavy downpours will be the primary threats from
today's stronger convection.

The bulk of the stronger thunderstorms will move out of the plains
by late evening. However, with the upper-level trough traversing
overhead, we'll retain potential for overnight showers and weak
thunderstorms. Increased PoPs notably for our northern areas in
particular. Will additionally need to monitor potential for patchy
fog Sunday morning across portions of the lower elevations,
especially the South Platte River Valley.

Sunday stands to be our coolest day of the week with the passage
of the shortwave. If we're able to clear out morning cloud cover
more efficiently, the environment would support renewed scattered
showers/t-storms in the afternoon and evening. It's a big if, with
the convective potential being notably lower for the northern half
of our forecast area, and best for the Palmer Divide and areas
downstream into Lincoln County where it would be easiest to erode
any low-level capping. Depending on how quickly the low ejects to
our east, isolated to scattered late-day showers and thunderstorms
could linger into Monday, but any coverage should be notably
reduced relative to previous days.

Starting Tuesday, warmer conditions will return as a southwest
flow pattern takes hold aloft. An embedded shortwave late Tuesday
into Wednesday favors an increase in precipitation potential
namely for our mountains, with lesser coverage/more uncertainty
for the lower elevations. Regardless, moisture profiles won't be
as robust as those currently being observed, so accumulations
should be on the lighter side if we see any.

KDEN gates, though isolated -SHRA may linger for an additional 1-2

.SHORT TERM...
(Now through Tuesday)
Issued at 1115 AM CDT Sat Sep 19 2026

A strong upper ridge remains centered over northeast Texas while a 
weak upper low continues to move westward across Florida toward the 
eastern Gulf. At the surface, high pressure remains nearby with 
clear skies and generally light or calm winds across the area. The 
upper low will make little westward progress toward the local area 
today as the ridge remains firmly in control, maintaining strong 
subsidence and a very dry column above the boundary layer. As a 
result, today will be another mostly sunny and hot day with 
essentially no meaningful rain chances. Highs should reach the lower 
90 to mid 90s, with a few locations around Baton Rouge metro and 
southwest Mississippi approaching the upper 90s. These values are 
several degrees above normal and near daily records at a few 
locations, although most sites should remain just below record 
levels. Increasing low-level moisture compared to Friday will also 
push afternoon heat indices back toward or above 100 degrees in more 
areas than not, but values should remain below Heat Advisory 
criteria.

Basically no changes through Sunday as the ridge continues to 
provide the dominant influence over the region. However, the surface 
ridge shifting closer to the northern Gulf Coast will allow low-
level moisture to gradually increase. This will be most noticeable 
in dewpoints and heat indices. Highs again will soar into the mid 
90s across much of the CWA and peak heat indices top out generally 
in the 100 to 106 degree range. A few localized spots could briefly 
approach the 108 degree Heat Advisory threshold, but currently looks 
like insufficient coverage and duration for a headline. Rain chances 
will remain very low across most of the area. The exception may be 
the Mississippi coast and adjacent waters where enough moisture may 
reach the western periphery of the eastern Gulf upper low to support 
a very isolated afternoon shower or thunderstorm.

The first more noticeable change in the forecast arrives Monday as a 
northern-stream shortwave tracks across the northern Plains toward 
the upper Mississippi Valley. Doing this helps flatten/weaken the 
northern and eastern side of the upper ridge aloft. At the same 
time, continued low-level moisture return and decreasing subsidence 
should allow a more substantial recovery in column moisture. This 
should be enough to bring back a more typical late-summer diurnal 
convective pattern, although coverage still looks fairly limited. 
Expect isolated to scattered showers and thunderstorms to develop 
first near the coast along seabreeze boundaries before spreading 
inland during the afternoon. Coverage should generally remain 
highest across the coastal half of southeast Louisiana and southern 
Mississippi, with lower chances farther northwest toward Baton Rouge 
and southwest Mississippi. Temperatures Monday will remain well 
above normal, with highs generally in the lower to mid 90s before 
convection develops. Heat indices may again reach the lower to 
middle 100s and could briefly approach advisory criteria in a few 
locations if convection is delayed. Any showers or storms would 
quickly interrupt the heat, making duration and areal coverage the 
main limiting factors for a heat headline. Organized severe weather 
is not currently indicated. Locally heavy downpours will be possible 
with individual storms, but limited convective coverage and the 
absence of a focused low-level boundary should keep any training or 
flooding concern quite low.

.LONG TERM...
(Tuesday night through Friday)
Issued at 1115 AM CDT Sat Sep 19 2026

The trend in the extended forecast has shifted back toward a warmer 
and drier solution. By Tuesday, the northern-stream shortwave will 
be moving toward the Great Lakes while the weakening upper low in 
the eastern Gulf begins to lift northeastward. Rather than allowing 
a deeper trough to become established over the eastern CONUS, the 
upper ridge is now expected to rebuild eastward from Texas and the 
southern Plains. There could still be enough residual moisture and 
weak daytime convergence Tuesday for an isolated afternoon shower or 
storm, particularly closer to the coast, but the rebuilding ridge 
should increasingly suppress convection from Tuesday into Wednesday. 
That trend looks to continue the remainder of the forecast period 
and end of next week as ridging remains the dominant feature aloft. 
The best moisture and instability should become confined to the 
coastal waters with mainly dry conditions across most land areas. 
The persistence of the ridge will also keep temperatures above late-
September normals. Highs should remain mainly in the lower to middle 
90s Tuesday and Wednesday. A gradually increasing northeasterly low-
level component may trim temperatures by a few degrees Thursday and 
Friday, but no meaningful cool-down is currently expected. Overnight 
lows will generally remain in the lower to middle 70s inland and 
middle to upper 70s near the coast and tidal lakes as warm water 
augments temps.

.DISCUSSION...

High pressure shifts away from the region late tonight as a low
organizes and develops over the Midwest. The warm front
associated with this low may briefly lift into the region on
Sunday, but will be quickly followed by a cold front Sunday
Night into Monday Morning. 

Regardless of the exact evolution of the warm front, should
start to see rain showers move into the region by late this
evening in response to modest mid and upper level synoptic scale
lift associate with the cyclogensis. 

As far as hazards, there remains a concern for localized flash
flooding, particularly in urban areas, however that threat has
decreased slightly. At the surface, a persistent easterly flow 
will be in place through tomorrow, gradually becoming 
southeasterly. As such, low level moisture will be on the 
increase, with surface dew points rising well into the 60s and 
precipitable water values increasing to near 2 inches.
Precipitable water values that high are well above the 90th
percentile. 

Most models have trended faster with the low and then front 
sweeping through the region. This is the main factor why 
forecasted rain amounts now range from 0.1 to 1.5 inches from 
Tonight through Monday. Additionally, the mid and upper level
synoptic scale lift never really line up with low level
frontogenesis, thus limiting lift.

The risk for excessive rainfall is a marginal, or 1 out of 4, 
through this period. However, with abundant moisture, locally 
heavy rain will still be possible, and if it occurs over urban 
and other poor drainage areas, localized flash flooding is 
possible. Additionally, if the warm front is able to lift into 
our region, areas along and south of the warm front could have 

The risk for other thunderstorm hazards is low due to very
limited instability.


KEY MESSAGE 2...A stationary front south of the region could 
keep rain chances around, especially for Delmarva through mid 
week.

Once the cold front sweeps through on Monday, it is expected to
stall south of our region. How far south that front stalls will
be a big factor in how much rain we see through the week. The
further south it stalls, the less likely our region will see
continued rain chances through mid week. Regardless, our region
should generally be on the cool side of the front through this
period keeping temperatures below normal and low level moisture
lower than what it is expected to be on Sunday. 

An upper level low digging in from the northwest could spark 
another round of cyclogensis by Wednesday, which could result in
the stationary front sliding north as a warm front briefly,
though it will still likely stay south of our region.


KEY MESSAGE 3...A closed low could develop off our coast by 
Thursday, potentially bringing another chance for rain, and 
increasing the risk for coastal flooding.

As early as Tuesday, there looks to be an inverted surface
trough off the coast of the Carolinas. However, most models
don't show this low closing off until Wednesday or Thursday.
That is not the only way the models differ; there are
significant differences in the track of the low, ranging from
the GFS showing the center of the low as close as 120 miles from
our coast, to the ICON, with the center of the low getting no
closer than 500 miles from our coast! 

The closer the track of this low is to the coast, the more
likely our region is to see rain, and gusty winds in the
Thursday and Friday time period.

.SHORT TERM /TODAY THROUGH SUNDAY/...
Upper-level water vapor satellite imagery early this morning shows a

continue across the region today before going more westerly 
tomorrow as the aforementioned low pressure system moves eastward
into the northern Plains. As the drying continues PWATs are 
expected to bottom out late tonight around 0.3-0.6". We will 
finally see this drier air make its way to the surface today as 
dew points fall into the 30s and 40s by late this afternoon/early 
this evening. There will be some moisture return from the Gulf of 
California into far SW AZ and SE CA tomorrow with dew points going
back into the 50s for them, otherwise dew points will generally 
be in the 40s for most other locations. Due to all the dry air 
across our region this weekend, there will be mostly clear skies 
with zero chances for showers or storms. Additionally H5 heights 
will remain largely unchanged (generally around 588 dm), so 
temperatures will also remain fairly steady through the weekend. 
Afternoon highs will be in the upper 90s to low 100s (upper 80s to
mid 90s) with morning lows in the 70s to around 80 degrees (mid 
60s to low 70s) across the lower deserts (higher terrain). This 
will result in widespread Minor HeatRisk across the CWA.

.LONG TERM /MONDAY THROUGH FRIDAY/...
Models are in good agreement that a Pacific low will move to the 
south-central coast of California by early Monday and then move 
eastward onshore throughout the day. If it weren't for the lack of 
moisture on Monday it would be a decent set up for a transitional 
severe weather event as there will be potential for some 
frontogenesis with upper-level jet support and higher shear. 
However, while PWATs will increase on Monday, they look to remain 
around or slightly below 1" (0.6-1.0"). 

Then on Tuesday the low will slowly weaken as it moves NE into NV/UT 
before getting swept up into the large scale flow on Wednesday as it 
moves into the northern Plains. At the same time a weak ridge will 
be in place over TX and will start to strengthen on Wednesday. This 
will result in southwesterly flow over our area. With the moisture 
return and some upper-level forcing from the aforementioned low, 
rain chances will return to the higher terrain areas in northern 
and eastern Arizona. Weak large scale troughing will remain 
across the eastern Pacific/West Coast through the end of next week
and will be battling the ridge of high pressure over TX. By the 
end of the workweek the ridge will try to retrograde into NM/AZ. 
Additionally ensemble members bring a surge of moisture into our 
area from the SE pushing PWATs back into a 1.0-1.3" range. As a 
result NBM/WPC PoPs for the end of next week have 30-50% chance

County and around 10-20% across the lower deserts of south-central
AZ.

upper 90s to low 100s across the lower deserts and in the upper 80s 
to mid 90s across the higher terrain. Morning lows will generally be 
in the 70s to to low 80s across the lower deserts and in the 60s 
across the higher terrain areas. Morning lows do look to start to 
creep up by the end of next week (more morning lows in the low 80s 
across the lower deserts). As a result widespread Minor HeatRisk

While the primary active zone of convection will be across the lower

that will move across the region during peak heating. The atmosphere
will become moderately unstable, but bulk shear will be on the 
weaker side. However, DCAPE will be around 1000 J/kg. So if storms 
become robust, then they will have the potential for strong
downdrafts that could lead to strong to damaging wind gusts. At this
stage the greatest potential appears to be across southeast Indiana,
southwest Ohio, and northern Kentucky. Precipitable water will be 
increasing to around 1.8 inches, so storms could produce locally 
heavy rainfall, but they should be progressive enough to keep any 
hydrologic concerns at a minimum.

Active zonal flow will remain across the region through the rest of
the weekend. Each wave of convection will be a little further south
than the previous one. So for tonight, expect primary activity to be
across northern Indiana and northern Ohio, but the southern flank of
this activity may move across northern counties. Parameters will be 
favorable for efficient warm rain processes, and northern counties 
still have the most vulnerable ground conditions due to previous 
heavy rainfall. It appears that activity will be progressive with a 
limited potential for repeated rounds of rainfall, as may occur just 
a bit further north. But this will have to be monitored closely in 
case there are any southward adjustments to the more active 
convective corridor.

Weak low pressure and a cold front will move across the forecast 
area Sunday afternoon and evening. Another round of showers and
some thunderstorms will occur along and north of the front. There
will still be a heavy rain threat with precipitable water near 1.8
inches and warm cloud depth around 4 km. Greatest potential will be

.KEY MESSAGES...

* Unseasonably hot weather will continue for much of the area 
  through at least Sunday. Barring any early day thunderstorms, heat 
  indices will top out in the mid 90s to around 105 (highest 
  southwest) each afternoon.

* There is a 30-50% chance (highest northeast) for showers and 
  storms late this afternoon and evening, with slightly lower 
  chances tomorrow. Locally damaging wind gusts and heavy rainfall 
  may accompany the strongest storms.

* A weather system will bring higher rain chances (50-70%) Monday 
  into Tuesday, followed by a cooldown to more seasonable 
  temperatures (highs in the 70s, lows in the 50s) by the second 
  half of week.

&&

.SHORT TERM /THROUGH SUNDAY NIGHT/...
Issued at 310 AM EDT Sat Sep 19 2026

*** HOT WITH SCATTERED PM STORMS (SEVERE?) TODAY ***

Early Saturday morning, a quasistationary front, evident via a 
subtle dewpoint gradient, was situated over northern Kentucky and 
southern Indiana. In addition, a decaying outflow boundary left in 
the wake of last evening's storms has laid out near the 
Kentucky/Tennessee border. The former boundary is slated to lift 
northward as a warm front today, while confidence remains lower on 
whether the latter (outflow) boundary will fully mix out this 
afternoon or serve as a focus for a few storms. Convective allowing 
models (CAMs) are certainly more aggressive with thunderstorms along 
the warm front, but the ARW, HRRR, and FV3 try to pop a couple cells 
further south. Accordingly, we've maintained "slight chance" (i.e., 
15-24%) probabilities of precipitation (PoPs) in the forecast across 
southern portions of the county warning area (CWA) while boosting 
them to 40-60% further northeast where confidence is higher in a 
loosely-organized mesoscale convective system (MCS). It is worth 
noting that most guidance is hitting areas just north our of local 
area (central IN into southwest OH) with the strongest convection, 
but given the weakly sheared (0-6km shear ~20-25 kt) environment and 
potential storm interaction(s) with the aforementioned outflow 
boundary confidence is low in placement. Wherever this potential MCS 
sets up, modest buoyancy (MLCAPE 1500-2500 J/kg), PWATs of 1.7-1.9 
inches, and notable inverted V on forecast soundings suggests strong 
winds will be a concern, particularly with any bowing segments where 
wind production may be aided by a rear inflow jet (RIJ). CAM wind 
gust output supports this notion, with various CAMs spitting out 
splotches of 40-60 mph gusts, and a couple very isolated pockets of 
70+ mph apparent in the ensemble max. SPC maintains a level 1 of 5 
(marginal) risk for severe weather across areas east of a roughly 
French Lick, IN to E-town to Edmonton line, with damaging winds the 
primary hazard. Outside of storms it'll be another unseasonably hot 
one with afternoon highs solidly in the 90s for most of the area and 
dewpoints, pooling near the warm front, in the upper 60s to low 70s. 
This will result in yet another day of heat indices in the upper 90s 
to around 105, highest west of the marginal severe weather risk area 
where a Heat Advisory is in effect.

*** TOASTY AGAIN, LOWER CHANCE OF A STRAY STORM SUNDAY ***

The axis of the shortwave trough responsible for this evening's 
storms is slated to exit the local area early tomorrow morning, 
leaving subsidence in its wake. This should result in a drier 
planetary boundary layer (PBL) during the afternoon, when dewpoints 
may fall into the lower-mid 60s in many places. Still, it'll be hot 
with forecast high temperatures once again solidly in the 90s area 
wide - favoring yet one more day of Moderate to Major HeatRisk 
(highest southwest and in urban areas). In addition, we may once 
again see a stray shower or storm, with the highest chances in two 
separate areas: one along any remnant outflow boundary left in the 
wake of this evening's storms across the Bluegrass and another over 
southern Indiana/far northern Kentucky where a weak shortwave trough 
is forecast to provide lift during the late afternoon-evening. Shear 
is forecast to remain weak while instability is a bit lower compared 
to today, suggesting the risk for organized severe storms is low; 
even so, we can't rule out locally gusty winds in any collapsing 
taller core. SPC has areas near and north of the I-64 corridor 
outlooked in a level 1 of 5 (marginal) risk for severe weather.

&&

.LONG TERM /MONDAY THROUGH FRIDAY/...
Issued at 310 AM EDT Sat Sep 19 2026

*** LESS HOT NORTH WITH A FEW STORMS MONDAY ***

The ridge will begin to break down early next work week as yet 
another shortwave trough crosses the area Monday evening. This could 
spark a few afternoon and evening storms, which may once again carry 
some risk for severe weather, though fortunately global models and 
their respective ensembles suggest some displacement between the 
best shear (north) and most optimal instability (south); the Low 
Resolution Ensemble Forecast (LREF) system only gives a 10-30% joint 
probability for > 1000 J/kg MUCAPE and > 30 kt 0-6km bulk shear 
across western/central Kentucky Monday afternoon (and this may be 
inflated due to timing differences among LREF members). Depending on 
timing of the trough, cold front, and associated storms, the area 
may see quite the gradient in temperatures during the afternoon, 
with some locations (most likely southern KY) topping out in the low-
mid 90s and others in the upper 70s.

*** FEELING MORE LIKE FALL BY MID WEEK ***

Behind the front, more seasonable temperatures should overtake the 
region with highs in the 70s north and low to mid 80s south by 
Tuesday. Wednesday onward, raw (LREF) and calibrated (NBM) guidance 
agree temperatures are likely to peak each afternoon in the 70s and 
drop each night into the 50s - near to slightly below normal and 
certainly much more fall-like. This mild, dry weather is likely to 
persist at least through next weekend as the upper level trough 
slowly drifts from the Great Lakes into the Northeast, keeping our 
area under northerly flow/cool advection.

&&

.AVIATION /12Z TAFS THROUGH 18Z SUNDAY/...
Issued at 708 AM EDT Sat Sep 19 2026

IFR clouds and patchy fog have developed over portions of central

only airfield affected so far has been LEX, thanks to prolific mid-

Winds, light and fickle early this morning, should blow

with lingering moderate rain over most of the area. This
activity should linger into middle morning, before a possible 
lull in the activity by later this morning occurs. Ceilings
below 1000 feet AGL and visibility of 1 to 4 miles are generally
expected this morning, with gusty southeast winds gradually
weakening.

There are additional showers and storms with heavy rainfall 
remaining to the west and southwest of the area early this 
morning. This activity should mainly miss or just clip areas
southwest of Madison.

Another round of showers and some storms should occur this 
afternoon into early this evening across the area. The better 
potential for heavy rain should be for Madison and Milwaukee and
south. Lighter southeast to east winds are expected this
afternoon, as low pressure passes by to the south. Ceilings
should remain below 1000 feet AGL this afternoon and early
evening, with 1 to 4 mile visibility within the showers and 
storms. 

Showers and a few storms should linger into the evening,
gradually pushing southeast of the area later tonight into early
Sunday morning. Winds will become east to northeast and increase
by Sunday morning. Ceilings should remain below 1000 feet AGL
into early Sunday morning, before rising to above 3000 feet AGL
by Sunday afternoon. Visibility should be in the 1 to 4 mile
range until the rain moves out of the area.

.MARINE...
Issued 558 AM CDT Sat Sep 19 2026

Low pressure around 29.8 inches will move east northeast toward
far southern Lake Michigan today, then just south of the 
southern portions of the lake tonight. Winds will become 
southeast and gusty ahead of the low, then shift northeast 
tonight as the low passes to the south. Areas of widespread 
showers and thunderstorms will accompany the passing area of low
pressure today into tonight.

Gusty east to northeast winds are then expected Sunday through 
Monday night, as low pressure slowly moves into the Ohio River 
Valley. High pressure around 30.5 inches will move southeast 
into Ontario during this period. Gusts could occasionally 
approach gale force Sunday into Monday night, mainly over 
southern portions of the lake. Winds will steadily taper Tuesday
through Wednesday, as the high pressure system moves into 
Quebec and New England.

A Small Craft Advisory is in effect through early Tuesday
evening for the nearshore waters of Lake Michigan, for the
combination of gusty onshore winds and building waves through
this period. This may need to be extended into Wednesday
evening, if the high waves persist.
